blocks.text: Galatians 2 moves through two connected disputes. In Jerusalem, Paul presents Titus, a Greek who was not compelled to be circumcised, and reports recognition of distinct work among Gentiles and among the circumcised, together with a shared concern to remember the poor. At Antioch, he describes Cephas withdrawing from meals with Gentiles and argues that this conduct pressured Gentiles to adopt Jewish ways. The chapter then develops its claim about justification, works of Torah, faith, and life shaped by Christ.

Titus’s uncircumcised status makes gentile belonging concrete rather than abstract: the disagreement concerns whether a gentile body must be altered in order to belong. Paul’s account of the Jerusalem meeting also presents authority as negotiated: he privately explains his message, reports recognition from James, Cephas, and John, and describes a partnership that includes care for the poor. The right hand of fellowship signals agreement and partnership, but it does not by itself establish complete uniformity or a centralized institutional structure.

Paul says that Cephas had been eating with Gentiles, then withdrew after people associated with James arrived; other Jews and even Barnabas followed. For Paul, this separation had the effect of pressuring Gentiles to live as Jews. Yet the account is Paul’s retrospective, polemical narration: James’s intention, the visitors’ message, Cephas’s reasoning, and the outcome of the dispute are not supplied. That limit matters when reading Paul’s charge of hypocrisy: it should not become a caricature of Jewish food practice or a judgment on Jews as a whole.

Paul’s public opposition corresponds to what he presents as a public effect on Gentile belonging. At the same time, the chapter preserves a more complex picture of leadership than either unchecked authority or total independence: Paul reports both private discussion and public confrontation, both disagreement and partnership.

The ancient text does not mark where Paul’s speech to Cephas ends after verse 14. Readers therefore differ over whether verses 15-21 still quote his Antioch address or shift into direct address to the Galatians. Either way, the argument remains continuous: the table conflict leads into Paul’s discussion of justification, works of Torah, and life in Christ.

“Works of Torah” should not simply be paraphrased as “Jewish legalism.” The immediate crisis prominently involves circumcision and Gentile obligation, though the full scope of the phrase remains debated. Likewise, the wording often translated “faith in Jesus Christ” permits more than one reading, including faith in the Messiah and the Messiah’s faithfulness. These uncertainties caution against treating one later doctrinal model or one translation as the only possible meaning of Paul’s language.

The relation between Paul’s Jerusalem meeting here and the Jerusalem council narrated in Acts 15 is disputed. Galatians gives Paul’s first-person account, while Acts presents a later narrative with its own sequence and emphases. The two accounts may be compared, but neither should silently replace the other or be forced into an exact harmony.

Galatians’ argument about Torah and Gentile inclusion must not be used to support antisemitism, contempt for Jews or Judaism, supersessionism, or the claim that Torah is intrinsically evil. Paul writes as a Jewish apostle while arguing about Gentile inclusion.

The movement from shared meals to justification language shows that Paul’s argument is not detached from embodied belonging: table separation could communicate who was fully included. This helps explain why the Antioch incident carries such force while also preventing the passage from being used to caricature Jewish food practice or to demand coerced eating.
“I have been crucified with Christ” is participatory and metaphorical theological speech. It should not be read as glorifying trauma, encouraging self-harm, or requiring anyone to endure abuse.
